notes.meaning: The angel led Ezekiel out of the inner area toward the northern outer courtyard. There Ezekiel saw a block of side rooms facing the open courtyard and the outer wall. These rooms served as special quarters for the priests while on duty.

The building was about one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with its entrance facing north. That made it roughly one hundred and fifty feet long and seventy-five feet wide. Its long side ran east to west alongside the temple yard.

The rooms were built in three levels, with balconies or walkways facing one another. One side looked toward the inner court, while the other side faced the outer paved courtyard. This placed the building right on the border between the two courts.
An inside walkway ten cubits wide ran along the front of the rooms. It stretched the entire length of the building, providing a shared path to the northern doorways.
The top floor rooms were smaller than the rooms on the ground and middle floors. The balconies took up part of the upper space, so each higher story had to be narrower.
Unlike the open courtyards, these three-story rooms were not held up by pillars. Because the outer walls carried all the weight, each higher level had to be set back farther.
A protective screen wall ran along the front of the rooms next to the outer courtyard. It measured fifty cubits long, matching the width of the building behind it.

The side of the building facing the outer court was fifty cubits wide, while the side facing the temple was one hundred cubits long. The outer wall matched the shorter side to keep the complex neat and secure.
The lower floor had an entrance on its eastern end. Anyone coming into the rooms from the outer courtyard could easily enter through this doorway.
Ezekiel saw another matching set of rooms on the south side of the courtyard. They stood opposite the temple building and the open yard, just like the northern block.

This southern building had a walkway in front of it that matched the northern walkway in every way. The dimensions, exits, and doorways were identical on both sides. God designed His sanctuary with perfect balance and order.
The doors of the southern rooms matched those on the north side. A main entrance stood at the start of the walkway near the eastern wall, making access easy and orderly.

The guide told Ezekiel that both the north and south rooms were holy spaces set apart for the priests. In these rooms, the priests ate the most sacred offerings, such as grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings. They also stored these dedicated gifts here because the rooms were holy ground.

Priests had to change their clothes before leaving the holy area to go among the people. They left behind the sacred linen garments they wore while serving the Lord and put on ordinary everyday clothes. This reminded everyone that what belongs to God's presence is holy and must never be treated as common.
When the guide finished measuring the entire inside of the temple area, he led Ezekiel out through the east gate. From there, he began measuring the outer boundary surrounding the entire sanctuary.

The guide measured the eastern side of the outer wall with his measuring rod. In the Hebrew text, this side measured five hundred rods, making a huge outer border. This large space showed that God's future house would have ample room for His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars and translations translate the measurement as cubits rather than rods, following the ancient Greek Septuagint to match the physical size of Jerusalem's temple mount.

notes.meaning: The guide next measured the north side, and it was also five hundred units along the rod. This made the northern border the exact same length as the eastern side.
He then measured the south side with the measuring rod. It too measured exactly five hundred units, continuing the perfect symmetry.
Turning to the west side, the guide measured it with the rod as well. It matched all the other sides at five hundred units.

The guide measured all four sides, showing that the outer wall formed a perfect square. The wall served to separate what was holy to God from ordinary, common life. The square design symbolized that God's kingdom is unshakable, well-ordered, and completely pure.
